# Markdown and lists: settled design

## 1 What a unit's display markdown carries
- Unit kinds stay paragraph / code / image; a paragraph unit's display is GFM.
- Headings are paragraph units carrying `#`, quotes carry `>`; a list or table inside a quote stays in the quote's unit.
- Tables are GFM pipe tables; strikethrough is `~~`; task lists keep `[x]` / `[ ]`.
- A formula is its alttext as plain text, no delimiter.
- Attributions (blockquote footer/cite), `<dl>`, footnotes (refs and list) and self-links in headings are left out of the units.
- Inline elements with no GFM form keep whatever Turndown outputs.
- A list is one unit; nested lists stay inside their outer list's unit; ordered lists keep their numbers, including `start`.
- A list splits around every code block (`<pre>` / `<pre><code>`) or image inside it, at any depth, so the describer describes it; the part after continues the numbering and opens with an empty item at each enclosing level (compact CommonMark form `2.  3.  Item`), so resumed items keep their depth. Inline code stays inside the item.
- The title is the first unit, `# <title>`, built from extraction.title; no other unit carries the title; when the extracted title is empty there is no title unit.
- Not considered: image in a table cell, a table cell holding a list or code.

## 2 How an element becomes markdown
- One shared converter for every recipe; a recipe never converts by hand.
- toMarkdown serializes the element including its own tag (today it uses cheerio `.html()`, the inner HTML, which drops the tag: the cause of 0/53 headings with `#`, 0/16 quotes with `>`, ordered lists as `-` in production).
- A `<pre>` without a `<code>` child gets its content wrapped in `<code>` before conversion, so every `<pre>` becomes a fenced block.
- Turndown with the fixed config (ATX, fenced, `-`, `---`) plus the GFM plugin.
- The validator checks the units the recipe declared (real element paths, checks unchanged). Inside the same sandbox run, the runtime splits list units holding a code block or an image into list part / code or image unit / list part, converts each part with the same converter and prepends the title unit; the sandbox returns both the declared and the flattened units. The host validates the declared units; when clean, the flattened list is what crosses to the API and what the agent's extract tool shows; otherwise it is discarded.
- Not considered: telling code `<pre>` from non-code, empty markdown for a declared element, a table with no header row, Turndown's escaping.

## 3 What a recipe must do
- Prompt: markdown is GFM, hand toMarkdown the whole element; a list is one unit, never one per `<li>`, even with code or images; the runtime may split a unit into several and the extract tool shows the split result; formulas as plain alttext, no delimiter; leave out attributions, `<dl>`, footnotes, heading self-links and any heading repeating the title, through the recipe's own includes/ignores (leftover check unchanged); keep task-list checkboxes.
- The author and revision prompts carry the same rules.
- Validator: an `<li>` without a wrapping `<ol>`/`<ul>` is a problem, sent back for revision; no other prompt rule is checked; no check that headings/quotes/lists kept their markdown.
- Not considered: an agent failing a rule after its revisions run out.

## 4 How the spoken form is derived from the display
- Derived from display by walking its markdown token tree.
- Headings, quotes and the title unit are read as their words, markers dropped.
- Every block inside a unit is on its own line (newline); nothing runs together (today paragraphs and list items fuse: `'First itemSecond item'`).
- A list item is its own line, no full stop added; ordered items keep `1.` at the start of the line; nesting depth is not announced.
- A split list's empty item has no spoken line.
- Task checkboxes are stripped; struck-through text is read as its words with no sign.
- A table's header row is spoken on its own line, then each body row as "Header: cell, …" on its own line.
- Code and image units keep their current spoken forms and the describer.
- Sanitize tail: keeps stripping leftover emphasis/code markers (still needed for run-in emphasis from Turndown); an asterisk only when it touches text; keeps newlines; only a `<word>` pair reduces to its word; then operator sequences become words, longest match first: `<=` less than or equal to, `>=` greater than or equal to, `->` to, `=>` to, `<-` from, `<<` much less than, `>>` much greater than, `<3` heart, `<` less than, `>` greater than. The describer's output runs through the same tail.
- Not considered: formula LaTeX read character by character, a line inside a unit with nothing to pronounce.

## 5 How line structure reaches the audio
- One spoken string per unit, lines separated by newlines; the synthesizer's input shape is unchanged; tts/ does not change.
- Kokoro splits at newlines by default and the service joins the line audio with no gap; the newline is not named in the TTS contract.
- The inter-unit pause and one timing window per unit are unchanged.
- Not considered: very long lists split into Kokoro's own chunks, consecutive blank lines.

## 6 How existing recipes and items get the new behaviour
- Runtime changes reach every stored recipe on its next run.
- The four recipes that break the new rules (blog.dyanacek.com, newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com, harper.blog, ngrislain.github.io; see reports/recipe-audit.md) are edited by hand during implementation, overwriting their stored version row, going live with the runtime change.
- A stored recipe that fails the validator on a later run goes to the revision agent with bounded retries (existing behaviour).
- Not considered: regenerating already-extracted items, jobs running during the deploy, release order of pipeline and API.

## Documentation plan (settled)
Stale-info report: reports/docs-stale.md.

| Note | Action |
|---|---|
| technical-design/markdown-units.md | new: branches 1 and 2 |
| technical-design/README.md | add the new note's row |
| technical-design/recipes.md | update: validator check, prompt rules, scope "one element per unit" to what a recipe declares (the runtime splits afterwards); point to the new note |
| technical-design/extraction-service.md | update: toMarkdown serializes the element itself + pre wrap, the split after validation, the title unit |
| technical-design/article-extraction.md | update: spoken-form derivation and sanitize tail; remove the comparison-operator entry from what is not built yet |
| technical-design/tts-service.md | update: callout that lines within a unit come from Kokoro's default newline split |
| technical-design/item-contract.md | minimum: the title is the first unit |
| technical-design/the-describer.md | minimum: the sanitize tail's asterisk and operator rules apply to described sentences |
| product-design/what-gets-read-aloud.md | update: lists, numbers, tables, checkboxes, strikethrough, operators, title; fix "a list item reads as its own sentence, marker dropped"; remove the operator entry from what is not built yet |

# Program architecture (settled)

1. Distribution: pipeline/ and api/ change, tts/ unchanged, no new package. `@truto/turndown-plugin-gfm` added next to turndown 7.2.4 and reaches the sandbox through the generated injection bundle. Each deployable ships through its own CI. Tests in each tree's existing test folder. After the pipeline deploy, the four recipes (blog.dyanacek.com, newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com, harper.blog, ngrislain.github.io) are pulled from production, edited, tested through the new runtime against a page of their domain, and their rows overwritten through the Railway CLI; no copies kept.
2. One recipe run: one sandbox call; the recipe runs, then in the same call the runtime splits list units holding pre/img/figure/picture/svg, converts the parts, prepends the title unit (none when the title is empty); the reply carries the title, the declared units (with paths) and the flattened units. The host validates the declared units; clean -> returns the flattened units (to the workflow and the extract tool alike); problems -> returns the report, flattened units discarded. Turndown stays in the sandbox; the split counts against recipeCpuMs. Not considered: the split throwing (a throw in the sandbox presents as a recipe crash, i.e. revision), a list part converting to empty markdown.
3. Runtime contract: `toMarkdown(element)` serializes the element with its own tag, wraps a bare <pre> in <code>, Turndown fixed config + GFM plugin, trimmed. List split: paragraph units whose element is <ol>/<ul> holding pre/img/figure/picture/svg at any depth -> list part / code or image unit / list part in document order; parts are clones in their own <ol>/<ul>, the part after continues start and opens with empty items; an item that held only the block isn't repeated; image unit src/alt read as the element carries them (lazy-load resolution not considered; figure caption not considered). Title unit `# <title>` first, none when empty. Reply: `title`, `declared` (AnnotatedUnit with path), `flattened` (boundary units).
4. Orphaned-<li> check: a validator check on the host over the declared units; flags a declared unit whose own element is an <li>; its problem line names the unit (position and path), the list it belongs to, and the rule that a list is handed over whole; accumulates with the other checks; report goes to revision.
5. API: order unchanged (spoken form -> drop rule -> typed units -> images -> describer). Title unit is an ordinary paragraph (is_cruft only applies to image alt). `to_spoken` returns one string per unit with \n between blocks; the walk parses strikethrough and strips task checkboxes, numbers ordered items, header row then body rows each on a line, no line for an empty item; `sanitize_spoken` keeps newlines, marker only when touching text, tag shapes, then operator words; describer output through the same tail. Drop rule on the whole unit; no migration. Not considered: operators inside inline code, [x]/[ ] in prose, items stored with old spoken forms.
6. Prompts: the rules go into RECIPE_CONTRACT, which the author and revision instructions both embed; plain rules, no examples.

Every recipe hands its selected elements to one shared converter rather than converting by hand ([recipes](recipes.md)), so the mapping from source to markdown is the same across every domain. Inside the sandbox, the runtime splits list units and prepends the title after the recipe returns; the host then validates the declared units and returns the flattened units only when validation is clean, before anything crosses to the API or appears in the authoring agent's extract tool. ## 📄 What a unit's display carries | Source | Unit | Display markdown | |---|---|---| | A heading (`h1` to `h6`) | paragraph unit | ATX, `#` through `######` | | A blockquote | paragraph unit | `>`-prefixed; a list or table nested inside the quote stays inside the quote's own unit | | A list, ordered or unordered | one paragraph unit | `-` bullets, or ordinals that keep the source's own numbers, including a non-1 `start` | | A task-list item | inside its list's unit | `[x]` / `[ ]` | | A table | paragraph unit | a GFM pipe table | | Struck-through text | inside its unit | `~~text~~` | | A formula | inside its unit | its alttext as plain text, no delimiter | | Inline content with no GFM form | inside its unit | whatever Turndown outputs for it | | A `
` or `
` | its own code unit | a fenced code block |
| An image | its own image unit | `src` and `alt` as the page presents them, no markdown |
| A blockquote's `
`/`` | left out | none |
| A `
` | left out | none |
| Footnote references and the footnote list | left out | none |
| A heading's self-link | left out, the heading's own text stays | none |
| The article's title | the first unit, ahead of every recipe-declared unit; no title unit when `extraction.title` is empty | `# `, from `extraction.title`; no other unit carries the title |

> [!NOTE] Why the title is synthesized, never authored
> The runtime builds the title unit from `extraction.title` once it has every recipe-declared unit; the recipe does not select it. Building it this way is deterministic from the title the recipe already extracted, so it needs no judgement from the agent. The authoring prompts tell the agent to leave out any heading that repeats the title, so a recipe yields one title unit and the listener hears the title once (see [recipes](recipes.md) and [what-gets-read-aloud](../product-design/what-gets-read-aloud.md)).

### ✂️ A list split around a nested code block

```html
<ol>
  <li>Item A</li>
  <li>Item B
    <ol>
      <li>Item B.1</li>
      <li>Item B.2 with a code block:
        <pre><code>x = 1</code></pre>
      </li>
      <li>Item B.3</li>
    </ol>
  </li>
</ol>
```

comes back as three units, in document order:

1. a paragraph unit, the list up to the code block:
   ```
   1. Item A
   2. Item B
      1. Item B.1
      2. Item B.2 with a code block:
   ```
2. a code unit: `x = 1`
3. a paragraph unit, the list resumed:
   ```
   2.  3. Item B.3
   ```

The resumed part opens with an empty item at each enclosing level it needs to re-enter: the outer `2.` re-enters item B without repeating its text, and the inner `3.` picks the nested list back up at its own next number. The resumed part is valid CommonMark, and the spoken-form derivation walks the same tree the listener's page renders (see [article-extraction](article-extraction.md)).

## 🔄 How an element becomes markdown

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Sandbox: recipe runs,<br/>declared units with<br/>paths, display from<br/>toMarkdown"] --> S["1 Split each list<br/>holding a pre or image,<br/>convert the parts,<br/>prepend # title"]
    S --> H["2 Both lists<br/>return to the host"]
    H --> V{"3 Validator on the<br/>declared units:<br/>inventory, leftover,<br/>nesting, orphaned li"}
    V -->|Problems| R(("Report to the<br/>agent: revise"))
    V -->|Clean| O(("4 Flattened units,<br/>also what the<br/>agent sees"))
```

`toMarkdown` passes the element itself, its own tag included, to Turndown with the fixed configuration (ATX headings, fenced code, `-` bullets, `---` rules) and the GFM plugin. Each Turndown rule fires only when its tag is present, so the tag selects the markdown construct: `h2` for a heading, `blockquote` for a quote, `ol` or `ul` for a list. `toMarkdown` wraps the content of a `<pre>` with no `<code>` child in `<code>` before conversion, so every `<pre>` becomes a fenced block.

Inside the same sandbox run, once the recipe has returned its declared units, the runtime splits every list unit that holds a code block or an image, at any nesting depth (1). The split yields a list part, then the code or image unit, then the rest of the list, in document order. `toMarkdown` converts each list part with its own list tag intact. The runtime then prepends the title unit, only when the extracted title is not empty. Both lists return to the host (2): the declared units, each tied to its real element path, and the flattened units. The same validator runs at authoring, revision and extraction against the declared units only ([recipes](recipes.md)) (3). When it is clean, the flattened units are what the workflow returns and what an authoring or revising agent's extract tool shows (4) ([extraction-service](extraction-service.md)); when it reports problems, the host discards the flattened units.

> [!NOTE] Why the validator reads the declared units and not the split ones
> The validator's nesting check flags any two units whose paths sit inside one another. A list-part clone from the split has no path, because the clone was never part of the parsed article tree. Validating the declared units, which are still elements at real positions, means every path the validator checks is real, and a split part never needs one. The split runs in the sandbox because the converter lives there, so it happens before validation.

> [!WARNING] The validator does not check that a unit kept its markdown
> Inventory and leftover-text checks confirm that every element in the container is accounted for and that no readable text was dropped. Neither confirms that a unit's markdown syntax, such as a heading's `#`, a quote's `>` or a list's numbering, survived the conversion. A recipe whose converter drops the element's own tag therefore still validates clean. In production, 53 headings reached the listener's page as plain paragraphs, 16 quotes lost their `>` and every ordered list came out with bullets, and every recipe behind them had validated. Nothing downstream catches it either; the reader sees undifferentiated paragraphs, the table of contents finds no heading, and the audio sounds right.

> [!TIP] Rejected: splitting a list by handing each item to the converter on its own
> Turndown's list rule reads the parent `<ol>` or `<ul>` to number or bullet an item, so an item converted alone comes out with no ordinal and no bullet. The runtime instead keeps every surviving list part inside a clone of the original list's own tag, so Turndown still numbers or bullets the items in each part.

> [!TIP] Rejected: wrapping a formula's alttext in `$…$` or `$$…$$`
> `sanitize_spoken` has a rule for each markdown marker Turndown can emit and no rule for a dollar sign, so a delimiter would reach the audio as a literal character. The alttext carries no delimiter at all instead, and reads as plain words in both the display and the spoken form.

## ⏩ What is not built yet

- **Telling code apart from a non-code `<pre>`.** `toMarkdown` treats every `<pre>` as code and wraps it in `<code>` before conversion; nothing distinguishes a `<pre>` used for plain preformatted layout.
- **An empty declared element.** The runtime has no special handling for a recipe-declared unit that converts to no markdown.
- **The display of a table with no header row.** The GFM table stays whatever Turndown produces for it; the header-aware linearization a table's spoken form gets ([article-extraction](article-extraction.md)) has no counterpart in the display markdown.
- **An image inside a table cell, or a table cell holding a list or code.** Neither has a settled shape.

# Extraction service

## 🔭 Overview

Extraction runs as a service on Cloudflare, separate from the item pipeline. The Python API sends an article and a recipe, and receives the extraction result and, when an agent authored or revised the recipe, the final recipe. The service is stateless over recipes and items; every call carries everything, and the item database stays the record. The TTS service stays on Modal, a separate deployable untouched by the move. The payload shapes belong to the service: the API declares its own mirror of them and adjusts when the service's shapes change.

## 🏗️ Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph inputs [API side]
    api[Python item pipeline]
  end
  subgraph service [Extraction service on Cloudflare]
    direction LR
    entry["Worker entrypoint:<br/>POST /jobs, GET /jobs"] --> queue["Domain-queue Durable Object,<br/>one per domain:<br/>lease + FIFO queue"]
    queue -->|"creates when free"| wf["Extraction Workflow,<br/>one instance per job"]
    index["Index Durable Object:<br/>job id to domain"]
    queue -->|"writes job id at enqueue"| index
    wf -->|"dispatch + read"| agents["Flue agents:<br/>author, revision"]
    wf -->|"runs recipes on"| runtime["Recipe runtime:<br/>cheerio + the fixed pass"]
    agents -->|"extract tool"| runtime
    runtime -->|"mechanical checks"| validator[Validator]
  end
  api -->|"article html, recipe or none, job id"| entry
  entry -->|"status + output"| api
```

The Worker entrypoint owns the HTTP endpoints and nothing else: two routes, translating between the Python API and the internals. Access authenticates at the edge before the Worker runs; the service carries no authentication code. The domain-queue Durable Object, one instance per domain key, owns per-domain serialization: a lease and a FIFO queue in its storage; it is the only creator of workflow instances for its domain, so a job id that does not resolve yet means the job is queued. The index Durable Object, one singleton, maps job id to domain: the domain-queues write the entry at enqueue, the read path consults the index for ids the Workflows API cannot answer, and the index's alarm sweeps entries past a cutoff. The extraction Workflow, one instance per job, owns the extraction sequence: run-and-validate the provided recipe, author when none came, revise when validation fails, end on the not-article verdict, and return the output. The Flue agents, one per prompt, own the judgement: bounded loops with retries, the runtime mounted as their one tool, one conversation per Durable Object, with durable turn replay. The recipe runtime owns deterministic execution: cheerio, the fixed conversion pass, the validator's mechanical checks.

> [!WARNING] Recipe source executes in a Dynamic Worker
> workerd blocks every direct path to running source: `eval` and `new Function` throw, `data:` URL imports do not resolve. A Dynamic Worker, in open beta for runtime-given code, runs the script instead, and the beta is the standing risk. The local half of the proof holds: `pipeline/test/dynamic-workers-proof.test.ts` runs real recipe source through the Worker Loader under vitest on workerd and gets the same extraction from two consecutive runs. The edge half stays open. miniflare's Worker Loader does not enforce `limits.cpuMs`, so the kill that turns a spinning recipe into a validation failure is observable only against the real platform, and that case is skipped in the suite and run by hand. The deterministic stack around it is proven on workerd: cheerio parses a real article in 8 to 18 ms, and the fixed pass converts in 2 to 19 ms with turndown over domino-parsed nodes.

## ♠️ What the service exposes

| Member | Answers | Who asks |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /jobs` | acceptance: `201`; `409` when the id already exists, the resume path; `413` when the HTML exceeds the ~1 MiB cap, rejected with no job created | the extraction client, at spawn |
| `GET /jobs/{job_id}` | the job's state and output, `200` always, the state in the body | the extraction client, on poll |

The create body carries `html`, the fetched article (required); `recipe`, the domain's current script (absent means author); and `job_id`, the caller-chosen instance id matching `^[a-zA-Z0-9_][a-zA-Z0-9-_]*$`, so the API's `itm_` ids are legal unchanged; and `domain`, the article's final host, which keys the domain-queue.

The state is one of `queued`, `running`, `complete`, `not_article`, `error`. `complete` carries `title`, `units`, and `recipe` when an agent authored or revised one; `error` carries the service's error string, the only diagnostic it emits. Absent members mean not applicable, never empty.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> running: accepted, lease free
    [*] --> queued: accepted, lease held
    queued --> running: the queue creates the instance
    running --> complete: recipe validates or agent settles
    running --> not_article: the author's verdict
    running --> error: retries exhaust or platform fails
    complete --> [*]
    not_article --> [*]
    error --> [*]
```

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class JobStatus {
        +string state
        +string title
        +list~Unit~ units
        +string recipe
        +string error
    }
    class Unit {
        +string type
        +string display
    }
    class ImageUnit {
        +string src
        +string alt
    }
    JobStatus "1" *-- "0..*" Unit
    Unit <|-- ImageUnit
```

A unit is `type` plus `display`; an image unit adds `src`, resolved by the recipe's lazy-load handling, and `alt`, which the recipe never invents. No spoken form crosses the boundary. The API derives it.

## 📩 A job's path

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as Python API
    participant E as Worker entrypoint
    participant G as Domain-queue - one per domain
    participant W as Extraction Workflow
    participant X as Flue agents

    A->>E: POST /jobs (html, recipe or none, job id)
    alt auth or size fails
        E-->>A: 401 / 413 - no job exists
    else accepted
        E->>G: enqueue the job for its domain
        alt the lease is free
            G->>W: create the instance now
        else the lease is held
            G->>G: hold the id in the FIFO
            Note over G,W: the unresolved id is the queued state
            G->>W: create when the lease releases
        end
        W->>W: run-and-validate the recipe
        alt validation passes
            W->>W: title + units
        else no recipe came
            W->>X: author, base prompt
            X-->>W: recipe, or nothing saved
        else validation fails
            W->>X: revise, iteration prompt
            X-->>W: recipe, or nothing saved
        end
        W->>G: last step: release the lease
        G->>W: create the next queued job
        Note over G: backstop, not the fast path: lease alarm
        alt instance dead or gone
            G->>G: sweep, pop the FIFO
        else still running
            G->>G: re-arm the alarm
        end
        A->>E: GET /jobs/{job_id}
        E-->>A: complete + output / not_article / error + string
    end
```

The workflow's last step releases the lease and the domain-queue creates the FIFO's next job; the alarm is the backstop for a job that dies without running that step. Acquiring the lease sets an alarm one minute out; when it fires on a busy domain, the domain-queue asks the platform for the running instance's status. When the status is ended or the instance is unaddressable, the domain-queue sweeps the lease and starts the next job; when the instance is running, the domain-queue re-arms the alarm. The domain-queue creates the instance before it persists the lease, both inside its single-threaded window, so a failed create leaves no lease behind.

## 🧭 The job index

A singleton index Durable Object maps job id to domain in a SQLite table. Each domain-queue writes its entry while enqueuing, so the write happens inside the queue's own step instead of a second moving piece in the route. The read asks the Workflows API first, which answers any id that has an instance; when the id does not resolve because the job is still waiting in a FIFO, the entrypoint reads the domain from the index and that job's domain-queue answers the state. Entries are write-once: the index's alarm sweeps entries past a cutoff, and nothing deletes on the read or create path.

## 🧩 The recipe runtime

| Member | Answers | Who asks |
|---|---|---|
| `run(recipe source, html)` | the title and the units, or the validation report | the workflow's run step, and the agents' one tool |
| `validate(extraction, html)` | the mechanical checks' report alone, over the recipe's units, container, inventory and ignores | `run`, on every execution |

`run` executes the script inside a Dynamic Worker: the injection bundle carries cheerio, domino, turndown and its GFM plugin (`@truto/turndown-plugin-gfm`) with it, the article parses inside because the recipe's `$` must exist there, and what returns is JSON. The script's `toMarkdown` calls serialize each selected element with its own tag, so Turndown sees the tag that selects its markdown rule. `toMarkdown` also wraps a `<pre>` with no `<code>` child in `<code>` before conversion. The validator is not part of the bundle; the mechanical checks run in the main Worker, so one implementation serves the workflow path and the agent tool path. Inside the same Dynamic Worker call, after the script returns, the runtime splits a list unit around any nested code block or image and prepends the title unit, and it returns both the declared units and the flattened ones. The validator checks the declared units; when they pass, `run` returns the flattened units (see [markdown-units](markdown-units.md)). A recipe that does not parse, throws against changed markup, or hangs until the CPU cap kills it, is a validation failure: the revision path's trigger, with its crash report as the validator report. A module that does not parse never starts the Dynamic Worker, so it cannot report itself as data; the load failure is recognised from the platform's own error, which names `recipe.js` in some runtimes and raises a bare `SyntaxError` in others. Only platform failures outside the recipe are `error` terminals: a Dynamic Worker that is unreachable, a bundle that does not load.

## 🤖 The agents

Each dispatch opens a conversation keyed by the job id. The conversation is disposable, carries no history from other jobs, and its prompts are self-contained. A retry of the whole run is a fresh conversation under a suffixed id. The bounds are one hundred turns, authoring one retry, revision two, set in configuration with the model; the model is flash-class, to be chosen by evaluation before the agent round runs. The settled reply is a script validated in-loop by its own tool calls, a not-article verdict from the author, or the agent giving up. The reply never carries units. The workflow runs every settled script through the runtime, so a fresh recipe and a years-old one extract through the same deterministic path.

## 📞 The calling side

The API calls through a thin client: `spawn(html, recipe or none, job id, domain)` at the source step, and `resolve(job id)` on poll. The pipeline maps the states to outcomes and writes the `extraction:`-prefixed errors; the client translates nothing. The item's extraction handle is the job id, stable across retries. A retried item re-attaches to the same running job, and the API mints a new id only when the previous job ended `error`, because that is the one terminal whose instance would hand back the same failure. The item stores the extraction domain beside the handle, because a redirect can leave the item's URL pointing somewhere other than the final host, and the recipe insert at resolve time needs the true domain.

Fetching stays API-side and always uses firecrawl. The queued ceiling measures 300 seconds from `queued_at` and fires during holds too; each accepted retry restarts the clock. A `not_article` verdict fails the item permanently, and the retry route accepts the item under its cap, the verdict included.

> [!NOTE] The ceiling can kill an item mid-authoring
> An authoring that outlasts about four windows exhausts the retry cap, the item dies, and its job completes unread. The recipe the job authored is lost, and the domain's next article authors fresh. Accepted knowingly. Authoring inside one window is the expected case, the turn bound is a ceiling rather than a forecast, and the ceiling's simplicity is worth more than a paused clock.

## ⚙️ Platform limits

A workflow instance has no wall-clock limit; the bound is CPU per invocation, tens of seconds by default and configurable upward. The agent loops never approach that bound, because model turns are input-output waits. Instance parameters, step results and the returned output are each capped near 1 MiB: an article whose fetched HTML exceeds the cap fails as too large before any step runs. Finished outputs persist for the retention window, days on the free tier and a month on the paid tier, which is far longer than the poll's resolve cadence. Instance state is kept for that window too, so a job id is not reusable until the window passes.

--- title: "Recipes" summary: "How one agent-authored script per domain extracts the domain's articles into markdown units, its versioned record, how a URL matches to it, and how agents author and revise it." created: "2026-09-13" --- # Recipes ## 🔭 Overview A recipe is one domain's extraction knowledge: a script that receives an article's HTML as a Cheerio document and returns the article as a title and a list of markdown units, deterministically, so the same page always yields the same units. Agents write recipes. The first article from a domain authors the domain's recipe, and every later article extracts with it. When a recipe fails an article, that article triggers a revision. The model runs at authoring time only. ## 🧾 The script and its declarations A recipe is a script plus the declarations around it. The container selector names the element that contains the article, and everything outside the container is site chrome. The inventory names every element kind the domain's pages carry inside the container and the role each plays: a unit, inline content, a wrapper, or the title. The ignores are the selectors deliberately excluded, each with the judgement that justified it; typical ignores are ads, date stamps and share rows. Every recipe excludes footnote markers and footnote bodies, because the authoring prompts instruct it to. The author prompt and the revision prompt embed one shared contract of plain instructions. The prompts also require GFM markdown and a formula written as its alttext with no delimiter. The recipe passes the whole element to `toMarkdown`, never a piece of it, and declares a whole list as one unit even when the list holds a code block or an image. They exclude a blockquote's attribution, a `
`, a heading self-link and a heading that repeats the title, and they keep a task list's checkboxes. See [markdown-units](markdown-units.md) for what each of those becomes in a unit's display. The inventory is the union across the domain's pages, and an element kind absent from one page is normal variation across a domain's posts. The script receives the Cheerio document and `toMarkdown`, the fixed HTML-to-markdown converter, from the runtime, and imports nothing. The script reads the document without changing it. Domain knowledge enters as structural preparation of a cloned element. The script builds a `` for a table that lacks one, swaps MathML for the LaTeX in its `alttext`, removes footnote subtrees, and wraps a span-built listing in a `
`. The fixed pass converts the prepared clone.

> [!TIP] Rejected: the agent writes its own conversion
> A trial where the agent hand-converted html to markdown matched the fixed pass on quality and gained nothing by it: conversion stopped being identical across domains, and a recipe could get conversion wrong. The per-domain tricks survived as clone preparation, which is reviewable DOM structure, never a rewritten converter.

## 📦 Units and the fixed pass

Units come back in document order, one element per unit as the recipe declares them, never overlapping: once an element is a unit, everything inside it is that unit's content. The kinds are `paragraph`, `code` and `image`. A paragraph is any flow that renders as markdown: prose, headings, quotes, lists, tables; a list is a single declared unit, even one holding a code block or an image. The fixed conversion pass produces a paragraph or code unit's display markdown. Before the units reach the API or the authoring agent's extract tool, the runtime splits a list unit around any embedded code block or image (see [markdown-units](markdown-units.md)). An image unit carries `src` and `alt` exactly as the page presents them: the recipe never invents `alt`, and the src is how the recipe resolves the domain's lazy-load conventions. An image the article carries is always emitted, even when its src cannot be resolved. Acquiring, validating, describing or dropping images is downstream's business.

> [!NOTE] Why three kinds and not one per markdown shape
> Downstream distinguishes exactly three things: text rendered as markdown and read as prose, code that gets described instead of read, and images that get acquired and follow the alt precedence. Headings, quotes, lists and tables all derive their display from their markdown, so one paragraph kind covers them; even the read-along table of contents derives from a `#`-prefixed unit's display text, not from a kind.

The same validator runs at authoring, revision and extraction. It checks that every unit's element is inside the container, in document order, none nested inside another; that every element kind in the container is declared or reported as unexpected; that no readable text is left after the units and ignores are removed, with the leftover report naming the element kinds that carry it; and that no declared unit is an `
  • ` on its own. The report line for an orphaned `
  • ` names the unit, the list it belongs to and the rule that a recipe hands a list over whole. It also checks that every unit's markdown is valid: non-empty, no residual HTML outside code, balanced fences. Invalid markdown fails a recipe like any other problem.

## 💽 The recipe record

```mermaid
erDiagram
    RECIPE_VERSION ||--o{ ITEM : extracts
    RECIPE_VERSION {
        string id PK
        string domain
        int version
        text script
        datetime created_at
    }
    ITEM {
        string recipe_version_id FK "nullable"
        string extraction_handle
        string extraction_domain
    }
```

Each version of a domain's recipe is one row, in the item database alongside the items. A revision is a pure insert that updates no row, and the current recipe for a domain is the highest version, so the per-article read is one indexed descent. The `script` column carries the entire recipe with its declarations embedded, stored exactly as the authoring loop validated it and kept whole so a failing recipe reaches a prompt as one piece. `id` is a generated string following the house pattern. Extraction sets `recipe_version_id` on the item to the version whose script extracted it. That link traces a revision that made things worse to the items it touched. The column is null for items that never reached extraction. Recipes are global: one recipe per domain, shared by every listener.

> [!TIP] Rejected: a current flag or a separate history table
> A flag mutates the previous row and is denormalized state that can disagree with the version number; a current-plus-history pair overwrites the payload in place and duplicates the schema.

## ⚖️ Matching a URL to a recipe

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Article URL arrives"] --> B["Fetch it, redirects
    resolve"]
    B --> C["Host of the final URL,
    leading www dropped"]
    C --> D{"Any recipe version
    for that domain?"}
    D -->|"No"| E["Author one: the base prompt
    against this article"]
    E --> F{"Authoring succeeded?"}
    F -->|"No, after its one retry"| N(("Nothing: the
    item fails"))
    F -->|"Yes"| G["Save it as the domain's
    version 1"]
    D -->|"Yes"| H["Current version:
    the highest"]
    G --> R(("The recipe to
    extract with"))
    H --> R
```

The key is the host of the fetch's final URL with only a leading `www` dropped: subdomains are distinct domains, so `blog.exe.dev` and `exe.dev` hold separate recipes, and a canonical link declared inside the page does not change it. Consolidation comes from redirects: a hundred domains redirecting to one place all land on that domain's recipe. No recipe serves a set of domains, and platform-hosted hostnames with identical markup each author their own.

> [!NOTE] Why no recipe serves several domains
> Platform-hosted blogs put many hostnames on identical markup, and one recipe describing that markup would save every later hostname its authoring run. Sharing was rejected to keep one recipe per domain strict: a recipe's identity is its domain's key, and a set-valued key complicates matching, storage and revision for a cost, repeated authoring, that only platforms pay.

## 📩 The lifecycle: authoring and revision

First authoring happens when a domain's first article arrives: the base prompt runs against that article's HTML, best-effort within one hundred turns, with one retry of the whole run, and if that fails the item fails with nothing saved for the domain. A domain's homepage enqueued by mistake fails and saves nothing, and the next real article authors fresh.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor L as Listener
    participant P as Item pipeline
    participant A as Agent
    participant V as Recipe runtime
    participant S as Recipe store

    L->>P: Enqueues the article URL
    P->>P: Extract with the
    current version
    P->>P: Validation fails
    P->>A: Iteration prompt +
    current script + report
    Note over P,A: The domain is locked:
    its other articles hold
    alt the page is not an article
        A-->>P: The verdict
        P-->>L: Item fails, the recipe stands
    else a fix
        A->>V: Run the fix
    against this article
        loop within 100 turns,
    then two retries of the run
            V-->>A: Report
            A->>A: Fix additively, re-validate
        end
        V-->>A: Problems none
        A->>S: Insert as the new
    highest version
        S-->>P: New current recipe
        P->>P: The held item re-extracts
    with the new version
        P-->>L: Item proceeds
    else the fix gives up
        A-->>P: No passing version
        P-->>L: Item fails, the old
    version stays current
    end
```

Revision triggers when an article fails validation under the current version. The iteration prompt receives the current script, stored whole, and the validator's report. The standing instruction is additive: keep the recipe's previous assumptions and add what this article needs. The exception is a wholesale markup change, where the agent judges the domain was redesigned and may rewrite the recipe outright. Validation is against the triggering article only. The item that triggered the revision holds while the revision runs, then retries with the new version; the listener sees a slow item and nothing else. A revision that gives up writes no version, so the older one stays current and the next article from the domain triggers revision again. Each attempt is independently bounded.

> [!WARNING] A failed revision leaves the domain exposed
> Every new article from a permanently broken domain triggers one bounded revision attempt before failing, and nothing counts these consecutive attempts: the failures are visible, but the agent spend is unbounded.

> [!NOTE] The not-an-article verdict is what catches the 200-status error page

An agent looking at the page to author or revise reports the page for what it is. The verdict fails the item, from either prompt. From revision, the verdict also means no version is written and the recipe stands.

| Input | What it is | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| The article's HTML | Firecrawl's rawHtml for the URL | The fetch, which resolves redirects and so decides the domain |
| The recipe | The domain's current version, the script stored whole | The recipe store, by the matched domain |

| Output | What it carries |
|---|---|
| The title | The article's own title; the agent prefers the element that contains it, its judgement when there is none |
| The units | `{ kind, markdown or src+alt }`, document order |
| The verdict | Empty when extraction succeeded; not-an-article or not-accessible fails the item |

# Cassettes over mocks

The api suite replays a service behind an HTTP boundary, the extraction pipeline, from cassettes exactly as it replays firecrawl and gemini, so the client's real serialization and parsing run against the recorded shapes. Mocks are for calls that are not plain HTTP.

- Record against the real service when it can run: `wrangler dev` needs no account and serves on localhost. The conftest's matching rules carry the hard parts: body matching disambiguates POSTs to one URL, and repeated identical GETs replay in recorded order, which is a poll sequence.
- Fabricate when the service does not exist yet: a cassette is YAML of request and response pairs, hand-built from the boundary contract. The trade is that a recorded cassette is evidence the service answered, and a fabricated one is the contract restated as a fixture, so drift passes unnoticed. Both sides are ours, so the risk is small.
- The unreachable case cannot be a cassette: a refused connection produces no interaction. Point the client at 127.0.0.1, a closed port that refuses instantly, with recording disabled for that one test. The failure is a genuine network one.
- Mocks stay for what is not HTTP: modal's spawn-and-resolve, the gemini describer SDK.
- Volatile ids break replay: minted `itm_` handles differ per run. A registered matcher normalizes them on both sides, cassette and request, so one cassette replays across any mint.

# Agentic review

Cleans up a change so mahou:human-review spends its attention on judgment instead of on mechanical findings. It reviews for reuse, simplification, efficiency, altitude, and conformance to the conventions the wiki holds.

It does not look for correctness bugs. Those belong to the human pass, where someone can weigh whether the behavior was intended.

## Fixing without asking

`basics` says every decision belongs to the user and every choice goes back to them as a question. This skill is the exception, and it holds inside these bounds:

- It edits only files the changeset already touches, and creates no new ones.
- It fixes nothing that would change what the code is meant to do.
- It leaves everything uncommitted, so the user can read the whole pass with one `git diff` and discard it as a whole.
- It reports every fix and every skip.

A finding whose fix would break any of those becomes a skipped finding in the report, for the user to rule on.

## Step 1: Establish the changeset

Load mahou:changeset for the repositories, the base, and the diff. Follow the wiki indexes to the entries about the technologies the diff touches; the conventions facet reviews against them and every fix has to follow them, together with the project's `CLAUDE.md` and `.mahou/basics.md` when present.

## Step 2: Dispatch the facet reviewers

Five per repository, one per facet, all in a single message so they run together.

| Facet | Agent | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| Reuse | `mahou:reuse-reviewer` | new code re-implementing something the codebase already has |
| Simplification | `mahou:simplification-reviewer` | redundant or derivable state, copy-paste with variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind |
| Efficiency | `mahou:efficiency-reviewer` | redundant computation, repeated I/O, independent work run sequentially, closures pinning large scopes |
| Altitude | `mahou:altitude-reviewer` | special cases layered on shared infrastructure where the mechanism underneath should generalize instead |
| Conventions | `mahou:conventions-reviewer` | departures from the wiki entries and the project's standing rules the change touches |

Give each one the repository's absolute path, the base, the diff, and the path to write its findings to. Give the conventions reviewer the path of the project's `CLAUDE.md` as well; it loads mahou:wiki itself.

Reviewers write findings to that file and return the path and a count. Nothing comes back in the message body, which truncates long reports and costs a round trip to recover.

Spawn them unnamed and keep the `agentId` from each spawn result. That is what resumes them in later rounds.

## Step 3: Apply what came back

Read every findings file. Collapse findings that different facets raised about the same line or mechanism, then fix each survivor.

Skip a finding when its fix would change intended behavior, reach outside the bounds above, or when you judge it a false positive. Record the skip and its reason. Never argue with it.

Run the repository's linters and tests afterwards, scoped to the files you touched rather than the whole tree. The project's `CLAUDE.md` usually names the commands; when it does not, detect them from the lockfile or manifest and say which you ran.

## Step 4: Round again, up to three times

Resume each reviewer by its `agentId` and tell it what you fixed. It already holds what it reviewed last round and works out for itself what to re-read.

Stop when a round returns no findings, or after the third round, whichever comes first.

## Step 5: Report and hand off

Per repository: what each round fixed, what it skipped and why, and the linter and test results. Everything stays uncommitted.

Then hand off to mahou:human-review.

# Mahou

The agent is the magic: tireless, fast, and exactly as wise as the instructions it is given. The user is the spellcaster. They draw the circle, they provide the mana, they choose the spell, and the agent pours itself into the shape they drew.

No spell casts itself. No skill picks a library, no skill chooses between two designs, no skill guesses what the user meant. The agent brings facts and state; every fork comes back to the spellcaster as a question.

Skills stay small enough that the user can see what each one did and correct it, instead of large enough that they have to trust the outcome.

## Philosophy

Each skill does one job; when a skill needs a second job, it becomes two skills. A skill tells you how to work, while facts about technologies and tools live in the wiki. Nothing is committed unprompted; when work is ready, say so and wait.

## Rules

1. Never use the phrase "load-bearing".
2. **Never decide for the user.** Map the state, then ask. No recommendations, no leaning toward an option, no answering for them. Give a recommendation only when the user asks for one.
3. **Report what you found, not what you assume.** When something is missing, say it is missing. Do not fill the gap with a plausible guess.
4. **Never commit or push as a side effect.** A skill whose entire job is committing, invoked directly by the user, is the exception, because that invocation is the consent.
5. **One job.** If the work in front of you has grown a second job, stop and say so rather than quietly doing both.
6. **Never volunteer next steps.** Answer what was asked, then stop. Do not close a report with work the user did not request: no "still outstanding", no "you may also want to", no queue of follow-ups. If something blocks the job in front of you, state it in one line as a fact. Everything else waits until they ask.

## Code

Comments never go inside a structure definition. Object and array literals, payloads, config entries, test fixtures, interface and type property lists, props, parameter lists: a reader scans all of these as a shape, and a comment between two entries breaks the scan. When the rationale is real, it goes above the structure or at the site that consumes the value.

This holds in every repository, whatever the language.

## Scratch folder

Every artifact a skill produces for the user and keeps between rounds goes under `.scratch/<change-slug>/` in the project's root, never under `/tmp`: a design handoff, a prototype, a draft, a research file. One directory named after the current change, holding the files the skill writes: `handoff.md`, `design.md`, `research.md`, a `prototypes/` folder, a `reports/` folder, a `test-design/` folder, a `spikes/` folder, whatever the skill defines. A skill that reopens a file reopens it from there, so the folder survives compaction, restarts and the next day. Throwaway files that are not to be reused, such as a diagram written only to validate it, may still use `/tmp`.

Skills say "the change's scratch folder" and name only the path inside it.

## The wiki

Knowledge about technologies and tools, their gotchas and their patterns, lives in mahou:wiki, indexed one level per folder so entries load on demand. Load it now and read its root indexes, global and local, so that you know which topics have entries when they come up in conversation. Read an entry only when the skill you are running says so, or when the user asks for a check against the conventions for a technology. Do not bring an entry's conventions into a question the user has not asked; when a topic with an entry comes up in a decision, say the entry exists and offer to read it.

The wiki is the standard the conventions reviewer measures a change against. mahou:learn writes it.

## The project's docs

Projects mahou runs in keep their own documentation in a folder they own, usually `docs/`. How to find it and what its structure is made of live in mahou:docs, which every skill and agent that reads or writes documentation loads. Skills that do not touch documentation leave it alone.

## The local layer

A project can change how a skill behaves in a `.mahou/` folder at its root: `.mahou/basics.md` for standing rules, `.mahou/<skill>.md` for one skill, `.mahou/wiki/` for local knowledge. Every skill reads its own file when present, and local wins over global when the two conflict.

## Reporting to the user

When a skill hands the user a report, such as findings, an investigation's answer, or a summary of a change, it loads mahou:report. That skill carries the shape a report should take: what comes first, when to diagram, how to separate fact from claim, and the unslop rules to hold while writing it.

# Agentic review

Cleans up a change so mahou:human-review spends its attention on judgment instead of on mechanical findings. It reviews for reuse, simplification, efficiency, altitude, and conformance to the conventions the wiki holds.

It does not look for correctness bugs. Those belong to the human pass, where someone can weigh whether the behavior was intended.

## Fixing without asking

`basics` says every decision belongs to the user and every choice goes back to them as a question. This skill is the exception, and it holds inside these bounds:

- It edits only files the changeset already touches, and creates no new ones.
- It fixes nothing that would change what the code is meant to do.
- It leaves everything uncommitted, so the user can read the whole pass with one `git diff` and discard it as a whole.
- It reports every fix and every skip.

A finding whose fix would break any of those becomes a skipped finding in the report, for the user to rule on.

## Step 1: Establish the changeset

Load mahou:changeset for the repositories, the base, and the diff. Follow the wiki indexes to the entries about the technologies the diff touches; the conventions facet reviews against them and every fix has to follow them, together with the project's `CLAUDE.md` and `.mahou/basics.md` when present.

## Step 2: Dispatch the facet reviewers

Five per repository, one per facet, all in a single message so they run together.

| Facet | Agent | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| Reuse | `mahou:reuse-reviewer` | new code re-implementing something the codebase already has |
| Simplification | `mahou:simplification-reviewer` | redundant or derivable state, copy-paste with variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind |
| Efficiency | `mahou:efficiency-reviewer` | redundant computation, repeated I/O, independent work run sequentially, closures pinning large scopes |
| Altitude | `mahou:altitude-reviewer` | special cases layered on shared infrastructure where the mechanism underneath should generalize instead |
| Conventions | `mahou:conventions-reviewer` | departures from the wiki entries and the project's standing rules the change touches |

Give each one the repository's absolute path, the base, the diff, and the path to write its findings to. Give the conventions reviewer the path of the project's `CLAUDE.md` as well; it loads mahou:wiki itself.

Reviewers write findings to that file and return the path and a count. Nothing comes back in the message body, which truncates long reports and costs a round trip to recover.

Spawn them unnamed and keep the `agentId` from each spawn result. That is what resumes them in later rounds.

## Step 3: Apply what came back

Read every findings file. Collapse findings that different facets raised about the same line or mechanism, then fix each survivor.

Skip a finding when its fix would change intended behavior, reach outside the bounds above, or when you judge it a false positive. Record the skip and its reason. Never argue with it.

Run the repository's linters and tests afterwards, scoped to the files you touched rather than the whole tree. The project's `CLAUDE.md` usually names the commands; when it does not, detect them from the lockfile or manifest and say which you ran.

## Step 4: Round again, up to three times

Resume each reviewer by its `agentId` and tell it what you fixed. It already holds what it reviewed last round and works out for itself what to re-read.

Stop when a round returns no findings, or after the third round, whichever comes first.

## Step 5: Report and hand off

Per repository: what each round fixed, what it skipped and why, and the linter and test results. Everything stays uncommitted.

Then hand off to mahou:human-review.

# Pipeline efficiency review — round 3

## pipeline/src/runtime/injection/split.ts:150-153 (`blockHolders`)

The hand-written parent walk from round 2 stopped as soon as it reached an ancestor already in `holders`, so a shared ancestor chain was only walked once no matter how many blocks hung off it. The new version drops that short-circuit: for every block it calls `$(block).parentsUntil(list).toArray()` and adds every element the call returns, unconditionally, with no check against `holders` along the way.

Cost: for a list where several blocks (images, code) share a deep ancestor chain — an image gallery marked up as a list, or a list with a code sample in several items — each block now re-walks and re-collects the entire chain up to `list`, redoing work the previous block's walk already did. `parentsUntil` is also a full cheerio traversal call (it wraps each ancestor in a Cheerio selection and builds an array via `.toArray()`), so each of these re-walks costs more per step than the plain `ancestor.parent` pointer chase it replaced, on top of repeating steps that were already known.

Fix: keep the raw pointer walk from round 2 (`for (let ancestor = block.parent; ancestor != null && isTag(ancestor) && !holders.has(ancestor); ancestor = ancestor.parent) holders.add(ancestor)`), or, if `parentsUntil` is kept for readability, break out of the `for` loop as soon as `holders.has(ancestor)` is true instead of adding every returned ancestor unconditionally.

# Report

A report is what the user reads after the work is done: the answer to a question, the findings of an investigation, the summary of a change. This is not the design tree, the annotation loop, or a document going into the project's docs. Those have their own shape.

## Lead with the answer

State the answer or the conclusion first. The investigation, the searches, the rounds of questions that produced it come after, as support. A reader who only has time for the first sentence should still walk away knowing the answer.

## Diagram what reads clearer as a picture

A flow across components, a relationship, a structure with several parts reads clearer as a diagram than as prose. Validate every diagram with `superpowers:mermaid-validation` before it is shown; when that skill is not installed, say so and show the diagram unvalidated.

A pitch, a ticket, a doc can assert something the code does not back up. Say which is which. When a verified fact contradicts a claim or a decision already made, say so plainly, in the first sentence, not folded into a paragraph where it reads as one more detail.

# Validate

Proves a change against the running system, by hand, after the automated tests have passed. The tests prove the units; this proves the assembled thing does what the design said, through the path a real caller takes.

The rows come from mahou:test-design: every row marked `manual` or both, with its expected outcome and its setup. Without a test design, the user names the scenarios, and the skill records them in the same row shape before running any. The skill adds no scenario of its own.

## Inputs to ask for

Before driving anything, decide whether the surface under validation needs authenticated inputs, and ask for everything in one round, in plain prose in the reply and never through a tool:

- **An identity**, when the surface needs one: a user, an account, a token. Name the surface and what the identity must be able to reach.

- **Domain inputs** the change names. Read the project's docs for the kind of input its domain deals with, then ask for concrete values. The docs shape the question; they do not answer it.

A surface that needs none of these skips the ask. Do not mine the conversation for values the user did not give; the unconditional ask costs less than the recovery.

## The running system

The system is yours to bring up, not the user's. When it is down, say what bringing it up costs and do it following the project's setup once the user confirms. When a credential or a dependency is missing, stop and ask rather than working around it.

Everything runs against the local system only. Never against a production database or a shared environment.

## Mutating data to reach a row

When the existing data does not reach the code path a row exercises, mutate the local data to make it reachable. The discipline:

- **Capture the original value first**, with a read that prints what you are about to overwrite, before any mutating write. The revert depends on it.

--- 0 [paragraph]
# Review Before the Concrete Sets
--- 1 [paragraph]
Why the best review comments arrive before the pull request does, and what that costs a team willing to pay for it.
--- 2 [paragraph]
Every engineering org eventually writes a document called something like _Code Review Guidelines_, and every one of those documents describes review as a gate: a place where bad code is _caught_. That word choice is the whole problem. A gate is something you built once and now stand at, checking papers. It does not participate in the trip; it only decides whether the trip continues. Treat review as a gate for long enough and you get exactly what gates produce — long queues, resentment on both sides of the checkpoint, and a growing incentive to route around it.
--- 3 [paragraph]
## The gatekeeping myth
--- 4 [paragraph]
The myth is comfortable because it assigns roles cleanly. There is an author, who writes; there is a reviewer, who judges; and there is a diff, which is either acceptable or is not. Everyone knows where they stand. The trouble is that the diff already encodes a hundred decisions the reviewer never got to weigh in on — which abstraction to introduce, which invariant to trust, which corner to cut under deadline pressure — and by the time it reaches review, unwinding any one of those decisions costs an afternoon instead of a sentence. The gate does not fix the road; it just measures how far off it the car already is.
--- 5 [paragraph]
None of this is an argument against reviewing diffs. It is an argument against believing that a diff is where the decisive conversation happens. If your best reviewers only ever speak up at that stage, you are hearing their opinions **after** the point where those opinions were cheapest to act on. The good ones know this, which is why they leave comments that read less like verdicts and more like _questions you wish someone had asked **before** the branch existed_.
--- 6 [paragraph]
> A review comment that starts with "why" is doing design work. A review comment that starts with "please" is doing enforcement. Teams that only get the second kind have already lost the first.
--- 7 [paragraph]
That distinction is not cosmetic. It is the difference between a reviewer who is still curious about the problem and one who has already decided the diff is the problem. Once a reviewer commits to the second stance, the exchange stops being a design conversation and turns into a negotiation over how much of the original approach survives — and negotiations, unlike conversations, have losers.
--- 8 [paragraph]
### 1\. Grug brain considered
--- 9 [paragraph]
The [grug brain developer](https://grugbrain.dev) has a simpler theory of review, which is that complexity is the actual enemy and review is just the last checkpoint where a second brain gets to notice it. Grug is right about the enemy and wrong about the checkpoint. By the time a reviewer is staring at three new abstractions in a single diff, the cost of removing any one of them has already been paid in the author's time, and the reviewer's options have narrowed to approve, argue, or rubber-stamp. Grug brain smell complexity. Grug brain smell it too late, sometimes.
--- 10 [paragraph]
This is not an indictment of any particular reviewer — it is a structural observation about when feedback is cheap and when it is expensive. A comment on a design doc costs a paragraph. The same comment, made three weeks later against a finished diff, costs a rewrite, a re-review, and usually a little bit of the author's goodwill toward the whole practice of code ~~rejection~~ review. Teams that move design conversations earlier are not being process-obsessed; they are just refusing to pay expensive prices for cheap information.
--- 11 [paragraph]
> Consider two teams shipping the same feature. The first team writes the interface on a whiteboard, argues about it for twenty minutes, and only then starts typing. The second team starts typing immediately and argues about the interface three days later, in a pull request, across nine review rounds.
> 
> Both teams end up with roughly the same interface. Only one of them enjoyed getting there.
> 
> > And only one of them will want to do it again next sprint.
--- 12 [paragraph]
The nested point matters more than it looks: the cost of a review culture is not paid in code quality, which tends to converge either way. It is paid in whether people volunteer to go through the process a second time.
--- 13 [paragraph]
> Weeks of coding can save you hours of planning.
--- 14 [paragraph]
A review comment that arrives before the branch exists is worth ten that arrive after.
--- 15 [paragraph]
One engineering manager put it this way during a retro: the pull request is where you find out whether the design conversation happened, not where you have it. If review keeps surfacing structural objections, that is not evidence the reviewers are thorough. It is evidence the design conversation moved to the wrong meeting.
--- 16 [paragraph]
**A short digression on tools**
--- 17 [paragraph]
None of this requires exotic process. A linter catches `unused-import` and a type checker catches a mismatched `Optional[str]`, but neither one catches "this endpoint should not exist." That distinction is worth keeping in mind before reaching for tooling as a substitute for conversation: automate the part of review that is mechanical, and protect the part that is not. Press Ctrl+Shift+P in most editors and you can wire a formatter to run on save; there is no equivalent shortcut for "notice the abstraction is wrong."  
That gap is exactly where a design conversation earns its keep, so treat it as a distinct activity rather than a slower version of linting.
--- 18 [paragraph]
People occasionally write the literal string `<software>` in a design doc as a placeholder for whichever service is under discussion, and reviewers reading it later sometimes assume it is a real tag that got mangled by a broken template. It is not; it is a deliberate stand-in, same as writing `3 < 4 and 5 > 2` to illustrate that a comparison operator survived a lossy copy-paste. Neither example is a rendering bug. Both are exactly what the author typed.
--- 19 [paragraph]
#### Lists, structure, and the shape of an explanation
--- 20 [paragraph]
A design conversation eventually needs to produce something the team can point at, and lists are the cheapest way to do that. Here is a plain enumeration of what changes when review moves earlier:
--- 21 [paragraph]
-   Fewer abstractions get invented, because the second brain is present while the first one is still choosing.
-   Fewer review rounds are needed, because objections surface once instead of once per patch.
-   Authors stop treating reviewers as opponents, because the reviewer was part of the plan, not just its judge.
--- 22 [paragraph]
Compare that with the ordered sequence a team actually follows when adopting the practice:
--- 23 [paragraph]
1.  Write the interface, not the implementation, and share it before any code exists.
2.  Get one reviewer to argue with the interface, not the prose describing it.
3.  Only then let someone start typing the implementation.
--- 24 [paragraph]
Teams that already had four steps before this one keep their own numbering, which is why some retros number their action items starting mid-sequence:
--- 25 [paragraph]
5.  Add the interface decision to the team's running design log.
6.  Revisit it once, after the first real usage, not before.
--- 26 [paragraph]
The nesting gets more elaborate once a team tries to capture both the review checklist and the exceptions to it:
--- 27 [paragraph]
-   Mechanical checks
    1.  Formatting and linting
        -   Auto-fixed on save
        -   Blocking only if auto-fix fails
    2.  Type checking
        -   Blocking in CI
        -   Never waived, even for a hotfix
-   Judgment checks
    1.  Does the interface match the design doc
    2.  Does the change need a design doc it does not have
        -   If yes, review pauses and a doc gets written first
--- 28 [paragraph]
Some list items need more than a sentence, and forcing them into one loses the point:
--- 29 [paragraph]
-   Reviewers who ask for a design doc after the fact are not being obstructive. They are recovering, late, the conversation that should have happened before the branch existed.
    
    The cost of that recovery is real, but it is still cheaper than merging a structural mistake and discovering it during an incident review instead.
    
-   Sometimes the right response to a large diff is not a list of comments but a short script that reproduces the reviewer's concern directly:
    
    ```python
    def has_blocking_comment(review):
        return any(c.severity == "block" for c in review.comments)
    ```
    
    Attaching a failing example is worth more than describing one, because the author can run it immediately.
--- 30 [paragraph]
Some checklists arrive already fragmented, pasted out of a chat thread by whoever was taking notes, and the fragments only make sense read together:
--- 31 [paragraph]
-   a linter that
-   catches syntax
-   but never catches intent
--- 32 [paragraph]
Other lists are the opposite: each item is a small essay on its own, and splitting them further would only lose the argument each one is making.
--- 33 [paragraph]
1.  A design conversation held before code exists changes the cost curve of every disagreement that follows, because an interface is cheap to redraw and a merged abstraction is not; teams that skip this step are not saving time, they are borrowing it at a rate set by however long the abstraction survives in production.
2.  A review culture that only ever produces blocking comments teaches authors to under-scope their pull requests defensively, splitting one coherent change into five defensible ones purely to reduce the surface area any single reviewer can object to, which is a rational response to an irrational incentive.
3.  A team that writes its design decisions down, even briefly, stops re-litigating them every time a new engineer encounters the same tradeoff, because the record answers the question before it gets asked out loud a second time.
--- 34 [paragraph]
Some teams track the vocabulary of review itself as a small glossary:
--- 35 [paragraph]
And some teams track the same rollout as a literal checklist:
--- 36 [paragraph]
-   [x]  Design doc reviewed by at least one other engineer
-   [x]  Interface frozen before implementation started
-   [ ]  Retro scheduled for one sprint after ship
--- 37 [paragraph]
Occasionally the same list shows up copy-pasted from a slide deck, bullet characters and all:
--- 38 [paragraph]
• Move the argument earlier
--- 39 [paragraph]
• Keep the diff boring
--- 40 [paragraph]
• Save the interesting conversation for the doc, not the patch
--- 41 [paragraph]
##### A note on tables
--- 42 [paragraph]
Numbers make the earlier point harder to wave away. One team's review metrics, before and after moving the design conversation earlier:
--- 43 [paragraph]
| Review type | Median time to merge | Defects escaping to production |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gate-style (review after code) | 4.2 days | 11 per quarter |
| Design-first (review before code) | 1.6 days | 4 per quarter |
--- 44 [paragraph]
A second table, borrowed from an internal wiki page, never got a header row added — its first row of plain cells has been doing that job for two years:
--- 45 [paragraph]
| Tool | Strengths | Weaknesses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linter | Fast, deterministic | Blind to intent |
| Type checker | Catches shape mismatches | Blind to whether the shape should exist |
--- 46 [paragraph]
A third table carries its own formatting, because the practices it compares deserve more than plain text:
--- 47 [paragraph]
| Practice | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **Design doc first** | Write the interface before the implementation; see the [RFC tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Request_for_Comments) this borrows from. |
| _Pairing on the interface_ | Two engineers argue about the shape of a function before either writes its body. |

--- 59 [paragraph]
There is a version of this essay that fits in one paragraph, and it is worth writing down for anyone who stopped reading before now. A reviewer's comment is worth roughly 1/2n of its original value after n days of code already written on top of the decision it is objecting to. That is not a precise claim — nobody has actually measured the decay constant — but the shape of the curve matches what every engineer who has requested a late rewrite already knows by feel.
--- 60 [paragraph]

--- 62 [paragraph]
> **If you want the one-sentence version**

> Move the argument to before the code exists, and the pull request stops being where quality gets decided and goes back to being what it should have been all along: a record of a decision the team already made together.
--- 63 [paragraph]
None of this means review disappears. It means the pull request inherits a smaller job: confirm that the implementation matches the interface everyone already agreed on, catch the mechanical issues a machine would have caught anyway, and leave a paper trail. That is a much less romantic job than "gatekeeper of quality," but it is one a team can actually sustain, sprint after sprint, without anyone quietly starting to dread the review queue.
